# Write a Quick Project Status Update for Your Team with Le Chat

> **In short:** Paste your messy notes — what got done, what's stuck, what's next — into Le Chat, ask it to format a status update, and you'll have a clean message ready to drop into Slack or email in a few minutes. Le Chat drafts the words, but you still decide what to send. Note: Mistral now calls this assistant **Vibe** (formerly Le Chat) — you may see either name in the app and on mistral.ai.

By the end of this guide, you'll have a simple Friday-afternoon habit: drop your rough notes into Le Chat, get a tidy status update back, and paste it where your team can see it. This is for anyone who runs a project, leads a small team, or just wants to stop dreading the weekly update email.

## Before you start
- A **Le Chat** account (free or paid) — sign up with an email at **chat.mistral.ai**, or open the Le Chat app if you already have it.
- A web browser or the Le Chat mobile app on your phone.
- Your scattered notes from the week, ready to copy or paste — task tracker, Slack threads, sticky notes, anything.
- **Total time:** about 5–10 minutes from first click to sent message.

## Step 1 — Open Le Chat and start a fresh chat
Go to **chat.mistral.ai** in your browser, or open the Le Chat app. Look for a button like **"New chat"** or a **"+"** icon, usually near the top of the conversation list on the left side, and tap it. A blank chat box appears, ready for your first message. If you can't see a clear "New chat" button, look for a pencil icon or check the top-right menu. Starting fresh matters because Le Chat remembers the conversation, and old topics from a previous chat can confuse the new task. 💬 Example: just type **"Hi"** first to confirm the box is responding. You'll know it worked when a blinking cursor sits inside an empty text area and Le Chat replies to your greeting.

## Step 2 — Gather your scattered notes in one place
Before you ask Le Chat to write anything, spend two minutes pulling your raw notes together. Open your task tracker, recent team messages, sticky notes, and any email replies that mention progress or problems — anywhere with fragments of "what got done", "what's blocked", and "what's coming up". Copy the relevant bits into a single text file, or just leave them open in different tabs so you can read while you type. Think of this step like setting the table before dinner: Le Chat can only cook with the ingredients you put in front of it. 💬 Example: a notes file might say **"shipped login fix, design review tues, waiting on Sarah for API key, team retro Friday"**. You'll know it worked when you can see all your status pieces in one place without switching apps.

## Step 3 — Paste your notes and tell Le Chat what you need
Click into the empty chat box and paste your notes. Then, on a new line below, write a short, clear instruction telling Le Chat what to do with them. Be specific about the job — **"write a weekly project status update"** is much better than **"make this nice"**. A good instruction names the audience (your team), the tone (clear and friendly), and the sections you want (done, in progress, blocked, next). It's like giving a new assistant their first task: the more specific you are, the closer the first draft gets to what you actually wanted. 💬 Example: **"Here are my rough notes from this week. Please turn them into a short weekly project status update for my team. Use three sections: Done, In Progress, Blocked. Keep the tone friendly and to the point."** You'll know it worked when Le Chat replies with a structured message, usually within a few seconds.

## Step 4 — Refine the format if the first draft isn't quite right
Read the first draft carefully. If the tone is too formal, the sections are missing, or it's much longer than you wanted, just reply with a small adjustment. Le Chat keeps the whole conversation in memory, so you can ask for changes one at a time. For example: **"Make it shorter"** or **"Add a one-line summary at the top"** or **"Use bullet points instead of paragraphs"**. This back-and-forth is normal — most first drafts need two or three small tweaks before they're right. Think of it like editing a colleague's memo: it's faster to react to something concrete than to write from a blank page. 💬 Example: **"Good, but please cut it in half and put each update on its own bullet."** You'll know it worked when the new version matches the length and shape you had in mind.

## Step 5 — Make the draft sound like you
Even a great draft can sound a little too "AI" — over-polite, full of corporate buzzwords, or longer than your usual voice. Read it once as if a teammate had sent it to you. Mark any sentence that doesn't sound like something you'd actually say, and either rewrite it yourself or paste it back into Le Chat and ask for a more casual version. This is the step that turns a good draft into *your* draft. It's also a good moment to double-check the facts: Le Chat can sometimes soften a real problem, and you'll want to make sure any blockers are described clearly so your team can actually help. 💬 Example: **"Can you rewrite the Blocked section in plainer language? Right now it sounds like it came from a press release."** You'll know it worked when you could picture yourself saying the same words in a team meeting.

## Step 6 — Copy the final version into your team channel
Click and drag to select the whole final message, then copy it (**Ctrl+C** on Windows, **Cmd+C** on Mac). Open Slack, Teams, or your email client, paste it into the right channel, and read it once more before hitting send. A good habit is to add a short personal line at the very top — **"Quick update for the week"** or **"Sharing the weekly status below"** — because it signals that a human sent it, not a robot. You're not done writing with Le Chat; you're done using it for this particular task. 💬 Example: paste your update, then add one line above it: **"Hi team, here's where we are this week 👇"**. You'll know it worked when your team replies with reactions, questions, or a thumbs-up — and you didn't have to stare at a blank page.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting notes without explaining the job.** Le Chat is smart, but if you only paste raw bullet points, you'll get a cleaned-up version of the same bullets, not a real status update. **Fix:** always add a one-sentence instruction naming the audience, the format, and the tone.
- **Sending the first draft without checking the facts.** Le Chat may reword your *"blocked on the legal team for two weeks"* into something gentler, which can hide the urgency. **Fix:** re-read the Blocked section specifically and make sure the real meaning is still there.
- **Asking for one giant update covering three months.** Le Chat works best with one week or one project at a time, and the longer the input, the more it tends to summarize instead of stay specific. **Fix:** split the work into smaller status updates, or ask for a short "this week" plus a brief "looking ahead" section.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same habit — paste the messy stuff, ask for a clean version — works outside work too. A quick family recap, a trip plan, or even a thank-you note can go from rough notes to a friendly message in a few minutes.
- **For your business or work:** you'll save the 20–40 minutes each week that usually disappear into staring at an empty email, and your updates will be more consistent from week to week, which makes it easier for everyone to spot patterns over time.
- **If you're just getting started:** don't try to automate the whole status flow on day one. Just use Le Chat as a fast first-draft tool this Friday, see how it feels, and build the habit from there.

## Try it now
Open Le Chat, paste these three lines: **"Shipped: new homepage. In progress: pricing page. Blocked: waiting on legal."** Then type: **"Turn this into a short weekly status update for my team of five."** See what comes back — that's your first status update in under two minutes.
